migrationNotes: Spine: a head teacher turns two club lists into one list of every pupil, and the same stacking is followed from dropping repeats, to keeping them, to rows that differ in a label, to sorting the finished list.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-combine-result-sets-1 (how UNION combines its inputs), -8 (a numeric UNION count) and -9 (why UNION ALL returns order 101 twice). All three are taught on the first three screens; -5, -6 and -10 are the skill check.

lesson.title: Combine reports deliberately

lead.text: A join lays two tables side by side, matching rows and adding columns. The head teacher's job runs the other way. Both clubs hold the same kind of information, a column of names. What is wanted is a single longer column. The tool for that is UNION, which writes the rows of one query's result beneath the rows of another's.

UNION has two requirements. Both queries must return the same number of columns, since their rows are going to line up in a single table. The columns are matched by position, first with first and second with second, whatever they are called, so each position should hold the same sort of value. The two queries may read different tables or the same one, and their results can be different lengths.

afterFigure.text: The figure holds a single table, members, with one line for each pupil and club. Each club's query on its own gives four names. UNION takes those two results and returns the rows of both. Any row that has already appeared is dropped, so every different row is kept once, and that is how the head's eight lines shrink to the pupils who are actually there.

queries.label: Chess club
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Drama club
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

lead.text: Do by hand what UNION does with the two clubs' lists.

Dropping repeats suits a register, but not every report. A coach company booking places for each club's outing would want Cy and Di counted once for chess and once for drama. UNION ALL gives that. It stacks the two results and keeps every row, so a pupil who comes back from both queries appears twice.

The two forms differ in one more way. UNION has to compare rows to find the repeats, while UNION ALL simply writes one result under the other. The row counts follow a short rule. UNION ALL returns the size of the first result plus the size of the second. UNION returns that same total minus every row it drops as a repeat.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, UNION returns the six pupils and UNION ALL returns all eight lines, with Cy and Di twice. Both are correct. They answer different questions, so choose by what the count of rows is meant to say.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Keep every row
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION ALL SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

lead.text: Work out each query's list of ids first, then decide what UNION does with an id that both lists contain.

reveal.text: You removed the ids that both queries returned. Plain UNION counts each different row once.

queries.label: Remove repeated rows
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Keep occurrences
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION ALL SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: When two rows are the same row

lead.text: UNION decides whether a row is a repeat by comparing the whole row, every column of it. Two rows are the same only when each value matches its partner. If the club lists carried a second column naming the club, Cy from chess and Cy from drama would no longer be the same row, because the clubs differ.

That gives a way to keep context that a bare list of names loses. Add a label to each query to keep it. One query selects name together with 'chess' AS club, and the other selects name together with 'drama' AS club. The label is a fixed piece of text written into every row of its query, so rows from different queries differ in at least one column and nothing can collapse. UNION then behaves like UNION ALL, although it still checks.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the plain list of names gives six rows and the labelled list gives eight, because Cy and Di now appear once under each club. Whether you want that depends on the question. Include a column only if its value belongs in the report, since every extra column is another place for two rows to differ.

queries.label: Names only
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: Names and club
queries.sql: SELECT name, 'chess' AS club FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name, 'drama' AS club FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name, club;

lead.text: UNION compares the whole row. Put the id and the label together before you decide which rows repeat.

reveal.text: You compared the id and the label together. A label turns a repeat into a new row.

queries.label: Id only
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and selection label
queries.sql: SELECT id, 'paid' AS selection FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id, 'large' AS selection FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id, selection;

lead.text: A stacked result has no particular order, because UNION is free to return the rows in whichever order suits it. A report needs a fixed order, and ORDER BY supplies one. Written once, after the last query, it sorts the whole combined result.

Two things follow from that position. The sort runs after the repeats have gone, so it orders only the rows that survived. LIMIT sits in the same place and counts from the top of the sorted, combined list. Asking for the first three names from the two club lists, in alphabetical order, gives Ann, Bo and Cy, and Cy takes third place once, since the repeat was removed before the counting began.

afterFigure.text: Only the ORDER BY at the end sorts the finished list. The order of each query on its own is lost once the results are stacked, so there is no point in sorting them first.

queries.label: The combined list, sorted
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name;

queries.label: The first three names
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'chess' UNION SELECT name FROM members WHERE club = 'drama' ORDER BY name LIMIT 3;

lead.text: Back to the shop's orders. UNION removes repeats first, and ORDER BY then sorts what is left.

queries.label: Combined result
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First three combined ids
queries.sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' UNION SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount >= 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

lesson.orientation: Stack compatible results with UNION or UNION ALL and account for overlapping rows.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: The chess club has four members: Ann, Bo, Cy and Di. The drama club has four as well: Cy, Di, Ed and Flo. The head teacher needs a single list of every pupil who belongs to either club, for a trip permission slip.
Copying one club's list under the other gives eight lines. Cy and Di belong to both clubs and so are written twice. The head wants every pupil written once.

Each club's list is itself the result of a query. This lesson is about writing two such results one above the other and deciding what to do with the pupils who turn up in both. Along the way it works out what counts as the same line when a list has more than one column.

intro.promise: By the end you'll stack two query results into one list, and say which repeated rows stay and which collapse.

recap.keyIdea: UNION stacks results of the same shape and removes repeated rows. UNION ALL keeps every occurrence, and a differing column keeps rows apart.

blocks.text: You counted 6 names on the head's list, then found 5 rows under UNION and 7 once the labels differed. The third id in the sorted list was 103.

recap.nextHook: UNION made one list out of two. A list can also carry positions, such as who came first and who came second. Positions get awkward when two rows are equal, as when two runners cross a finish line together. The next lesson ranks rows and settles what a tie should do.

questions.prompt: How does UNION combine its inputs?
hints: UNION combines results vertically; JOIN matches related rows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: UNION stacks compatible rows from its SELECT results and removes duplicates. It combines rows vertically rather than matching columns through a join.

choices.label: It matches customer keys to order keys
It changes the stored table names

questions.onCorrect: It stacks compatible result rows. A join, by contrast, matches related rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Matching keys is what JOIN does. UNION stacks results.
UNION only combines results. It never touches stored tables.

questions.prompt: One query selects the ids of paid orders and another selects the ids of orders worth at least 40. How many rows does the first query UNION the second return?
hints: The two result sets overlap on 101 and 103.
Remove repeated ids from the combined result.
Take four paid ids and three large ids, then remove the two repeated ids.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Orders 101 and 103 are in both results and UNION keeps each once.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what UNION ALL gives. UNION removes the repeated ids.

questions.prompt: The paid-ids query and the at-least-40 query now each also select a label, 'paid' for the first and 'large' for the second. How many rows does their UNION return?
hints: Compare both id and selection label.
An id with a different label is a different result row.
The two selections contribute four and three rows. Their labels make even repeated ids distinct.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four paid rows and three large rows have different labels, so all seven full rows are distinct.

questions.onCorrect: 7. A different label makes a repeated id a different row, so nothing collapses.

misconceptions.feedback: The labels make the repeated ids different rows. Compare the whole row.

questions.prompt: The paid-ids query UNION the at-least-40 query is sorted by id, smallest first. What is the third id in the sorted list?
hints: Deduplicate before finding the ordered position.
Use the ORDER BY at the end.
Compare the increasing unique ids and choose the third position after deduplication.
questions.onCorrect: 103. UNION removes repeats first, then ORDER BY puts the ids in order.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be third only if the repeated first id counted twice. UNION removes it first.

questions.prompt: Query A returns ids 1, 2, 3. Query B returns 2, 4. How many rows does UNION ALL return?
hints: UNION ALL retains overlap.
Add the sizes of both results.
Evaluate 3 + 2; UNION ALL retains the overlapping id's occurrences.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: UNION ALL retains all three rows from A and both rows from B: five.

questions.onCorrect: 5. UNION ALL keeps the overlapping id, so the sizes simply add.

misconceptions.feedback: UNION ALL keeps the overlapping id as well, so nothing is removed.

questions.prompt: Which requirement applies to the SELECT results combined by UNION?
hints: Both results must have a compatible shape.

acceptedIdeas: They must have the same number of result columns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each SELECT must return the same number of columns, with corresponding columns representing compatible values. UNION aligns columns by position, not by name.

choices.label: They must have the same number of result columns
They must read the same table

questions.onCorrect: They must have the same number of result columns, so the rows line up.

misconceptions.feedback: They can read different tables. What matters is the shape of the results.
Text is fine as long as the columns line up.

questions.prompt: Chess club has Ann, Bo, Cy and Di. Drama club has Cy, Di, Ed and Flo. How many names are on a single list of every pupil in either club?
hints: Which pupils are in both clubs?
Write each pupil once.
Take one club's list and add the pupils who are only in the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Cy and Di are in both clubs. Ann, Bo, Cy, Di, Ed and Flo make six names.

questions.onCorrect: 6. You stacked two lists and wrote each pupil once. UNION does the same with two query results.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts Cy and Di twice. Each pupil appears once.

questions.prompt: Query A returns ids 1 and 2. Query B returns ids 2 and 3. How many rows does A UNION B return?
hints: Which id is in both results?
UNION keeps a repeated row once.
List the different ids and count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ids are 1, 2 and 3. The id 2 is in both results, but UNION keeps it once.

questions.onCorrect: 3. UNION stacks the two results and keeps each different row once.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds both results. The id found in both appears once under UNION.

questions.prompt: Why does UNION ALL return order 101 twice?
hints: Which of the two results contains 101?

acceptedIdeas: Order 101 is in both results, and UNION ALL keeps both.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Order 101 is paid and also at least 40, so both queries return it.

questions.onCorrect: UNION ALL keeps every occurrence, so a row in both results appears twice.

choices.label: Order 101 is in both results, and UNION ALL keeps both.
UNION ALL adds an extra row for every id.

misconceptions.feedback: The table has one row for order 101. Two queries each returned it.
Only ids returned by both queries repeat.

questions.prompt: A returns (1, 'x') and (2, 'x'). B returns (1, 'y') and (2, 'x'). How many rows does A UNION B return?
hints: UNION compares the whole row.
Which row appears in both results?
Remove the repeated row and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row (2, 'x') is in both results and is kept once. (1, 'x') and (1, 'y') are different rows.

questions.onCorrect: 3. A row repeats only when every column matches, so (1, 'y') stays separate from (1, 'x').

misconceptions.feedback: The row (2, 'x') is in both results. UNION keeps it only once.
